opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a question that comes up a lot, and my view has shifted a bit over the past couple of years. Early on, a lot of people assumed that vertical models, say a model built specifically for finance, law, or medicine, would clearly win in their own domains because they'd been trained on specialized data. What we've actually seen is that general models keep getting better so quickly that, for many tasks, a strong general model with good prompting or retrieval beats a smaller model trained from scratch on domain data.

So I'd frame it less as "vertical versus general" and more as "where does the real value come from." The base capability of reasoning, understanding language, following instructions is increasingly a commodity that the large general models provide. The differentiated value in a vertical comes from things like proprietary data, workflow integration, understanding of the customer's actual problem, and the feedback loop you build once you're deployed. That doesn't necessarily mean you need to pre-train your own foundation model.

Where vertical models still make a lot of sense is when you have constraints. Cost is one: if you're serving huge volumes, a smaller fine-tuned model can be much cheaper and faster. Latency is another, as are privacy and deployment requirements, where you need something running on-prem or on a device. And some domains have data that never shows up on the public internet, so the general model simply hasn't seen it. In those cases, taking an open-source base model and fine-tuning or distilling it for your use case is very practical.

So my general advice to companies is: start with the strongest general model to validate that the problem can be solved at all. Once you know it works and you understand your traffic and your requirements, optimize. That might mean fine-tuning a smaller model, building a mix of models, or adding retrieval. It's an engineering problem of finding the right trade-off between quality, cost, and speed, rather than a belief that one approach is fundamentally superior.

r001.rationale: It says companies may optimize with a smaller fine-tuned model and that they do not necessarily need to pre-train their own foundation model.

r002.rationale: It states that a smaller fine-tuned model can be much cheaper for high-volume serving.

r003.rationale: It notes that general models may lack data unavailable on the public internet, but does not clearly state that a vertical model may outperform a general model on domain-specific problems.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and my honest answer is that the framing of "vertical versus general" is a bit of a false dichotomy. Let me explain what I mean.

A couple of years ago, when general models were still weaker, there was a strong case for vertical models. If you had a legal use case, or a medical use case, you could take a smaller model, fine-tune it heavily on domain data, and it would beat the general model on that narrow task. And it was cheaper to run. That was real value.

But what we've observed, and I think the whole industry has observed, is that the general models keep climbing. Every six to twelve months a new frontier model comes out, and it absorbs a large fraction of what the vertical model used to be good at. So if your entire moat is "we fine-tuned a model on domain text," that moat erodes very quickly. You spent a year building something, and then a general model matches it out of the box.

So where does the real value in vertical domains actually come from? I'd say three places.

First, data that the general model simply doesn't have. Not public domain knowledge, which is already in the pretraining corpus, but proprietary data: your company's transaction logs, your manufacturing defect records, your customer interactions. That's where domain specialization genuinely helps, because no general model can know that.

Second, the workflow and the engineering around the model. In my experience building infrastructure, the model is maybe twenty or thirty percent of the solution. The rest is retrieval, tool integration, evaluation, latency, cost control, and making the output fit into how people actually work. A vertical solution that nails the workflow wins even if it sits on top of a general model.

Third, cost and latency at scale. If you're processing millions of requests a day on a narrow task, a smaller specialized model can be ten times cheaper. That's a very practical form of value, and it's often why companies end up distilling a general model into a smaller one for production.

So my advice is usually: don't start by building a vertical model. Start with the best general model you can get, build the workflow, collect the data, and figure out where it falls short. Then specialize, if and only if the economics or the data justify it. The verticality should live in the data and the product, not in a belief that you can out-train the frontier labs on general capability.

r001.rationale: It says a smaller, heavily fine-tuned model could beat a general model on a narrow task, showing that high general-purpose capability is not always needed.

r002.rationale: It describes vertical models as cheaper to run and says a smaller specialized model can cost ten times less for a narrow task.

r003.rationale: It states that a domain-tuned model could beat a general model on a legal or medical task.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between a model’s capabilities and the value of the product built around it. A customer usually doesn’t care whether you’re using a general model or a vertical model. They care whether you solve their problem accurately, reliably, and at an acceptable cost.

For a specific domain, a specialized model can have real advantages. If the task is clearly defined and you have high-quality domain data, you may be able to achieve better performance with a smaller model, which also means lower latency and lower serving costs. But domain-specific knowledge alone doesn’t necessarily mean you need to train a separate model. Sometimes a general model connected to the right documents and tools is enough.

The challenge is that general models keep improving. If your entire advantage is that today’s general model performs poorly on a narrow task, that advantage may disappear with the next release. So I would look at what remains valuable as the underlying models improve: access to useful data, integration into the customer’s workflow, and the ability to evaluate whether the system actually does the job correctly.

In practice, these approaches can complement each other. You might use a general model for interpreting a request and a specialized model for a particular step. I would start with the problem and measure the tradeoffs, rather than decide in advance that a vertical model must be better.

r001.rationale: The response says a clearly defined task with high-quality domain data may be handled by a smaller specialized model, and sometimes a general model with documents and tools is enough.

r002.rationale: It says a specialized model may achieve better performance with lower serving costs for a specific domain, explicitly identifying a possible cost advantage.

r003.rationale: It states that for a specific domain, a specialized model may achieve better performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between a vertical application and a vertical model. A problem can be very specialized without requiring a model trained specifically for that domain. A general model, combined with the right data, retrieval, and tools, may already solve it quite well.

So I would start with the problem and ask: What does specialization actually improve? Is it accuracy, latency, cost, or control over the data? If a smaller, specialized model delivers the quality you need at a much lower cost, that’s valuable. But being specialized doesn’t automatically make a model better.

There’s also a moving baseline. General models keep improving, so you have to consider whether the advantage of your specialized model will persist. Often the more durable value is in understanding the customer’s workflow, having good domain data, and being able to evaluate whether the system actually does the job.

My approach would be to start with a strong general model, measure where it falls short, and specialize where there’s a clear benefit. The goal is to solve the problem, and the model is one part of that solution.

r001.rationale: It says a specialized problem may not need a model trained for that domain and that a smaller specialized model can deliver the needed quality, implying a highly capable general model is not always required.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a smaller specialized model can deliver the needed quality at a much lower cost.

r003.rationale: It discusses cost advantages and says general models may solve specialized problems well, but does not state that vertical-domain models can achieve better performance.
